- Tokenizer regex: byte-identical, including U+2019 (bytes e2 80 99). The data has 0 non-ASCII utterances anyway.
- BIO parser: same as cell 8. There are no empty slot values and no leftover brackets. Minimum token length is 1 and maximum is 61.

Casefold averaging agrees with raw model.txt to about 1e-8 for also, first (including its ligature form), one, new, march, email and weather. Words with later casings past my 70k-line scan were not compared.
- Embedding init: RNG order matches cell 16 by reading. In the cache, PAD is zero, UNK std is 0.0515, all 4,731 pretrained rows equal the casefold rows, and the 567 random rows have mean std 0.0501. I did not regenerate the exact random values.

- BIOES: all 10,863 legal paths up to length 7 (2 types) read identically natively and via to_bio. Gold round trip on adjacent spans is correct. Invalid sequences do not crash and are read leniently, but only a linear head could emit them, and the ladder only runs BIOES with CRF.
- BIOES and biaffine metric path: predict uses to_bio on gold and decode_tags returns BIO strings, so all heads share the same metric. Biaffine was traced by reading only.

LEAKAGE, traced and clean:

The label adds 257 parameters to the linear slot head and shifts the init RNG for modules created after it, which is seed-level noise. It was predicted 0 times in all 9 saved dev frames. It cannot change any result beyond that noise, but it is technically test-derived and deserves one line in the report.

findings.title: Matched control copies one pool row per (n_tokens, n_gold_slots) stratum, so matched_gap depends on KD-tree tie-breaking
findings.claim: NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=1) (line 137) gets identical query coordinates for every Slot-Train-OOV utterance in a stratum, so it returns the same single No-Train-OOV row for all of them. On dev, the 215 queries fall into 39 feature combinations, so the matched set has at most 39 distinct utterances. Multiplicities reach 23, and the effective N (1/sum p^2) is 17.4. Test is the same: 341 queries, 47 combinations, effective N 17.7. Which row wins among hundreds of exact ties is an accident of the tree. The hand-off notebook (cell 42) has the same flaw. matched_gap goes into every dev_metrics.json and the leaderboard, and hand-off section 8 reports this comparison.
findings.failure_scenario: I rebuilt the frames from results/*/dev_pred_frame.pkl. The metric reimplementation reproduces the logged intent, slot F1 and subgroup F1 values. Flipping the one (4,1) row, which is copied 23 times out of 321 gold slots, moves matched F1 by about 7 points. With 2,000 random tie-breaks, Stage-1 matched F1 has sd 7.78 and a 95% range of 53.91 to 83.70. The Stage-1 to A1_fresh_lr5e-4 change in matched F1 has a 95% range of -2.35 to +21.27. Logged gaps against the stratum-weighted all-rows gap: stage1_baseline 43.27 vs 35.49; A1_ft_recipe 37.18 vs 37.32; A1_fresh_recipe 32.88 vs 32.15; A1_fresh_lr5e-4 29.43 vs 34.58; A2_slot2 27.82 vs 27.69. The logged result says A1_fresh_lr5e-4 closes the matched gap by 13.84 points against Stage 1. Over all tied rows the closure is 0.91 points. A report built on matched_gap would therefore state a gap reduction that is mostly an artifact. Selection is not affected, because family_table ranks on dev_joint only.
findings.suggested_fix: For each query, use all pool rows at the minimum standardised distance, each weighted 1/k, and pool the weighted TP, FP and FN. Alternatively, report direct standardisation over exact strata. Recompute matched_gap for finished runs from dev_pred_frame.pkl; no retraining is needed. Do not compare the result with the hand-off's 39.00 and 26.84, which came from single-row picks.

votes.reasoning:
The defect is real. I could not refute it, and the reported figures hold apart from three small corrections listed below.

CODE PATH
- experiment.py:149-150 passes the merged dev frame to matched_control.
- evaluate.py:134-135 gives 215 query rows and 1,669 pool rows. Row order is the same in every run: train.py:24 has shuffle=False, and ids and features are identical across all frames.
- evaluate.py:136-138 queries a KD-tree on two integers, (n_tokens, n_gold_slots). The search is deterministic and keeps the first row at the minimum distance, so equal coordinates return the same row.
- evaluate.py:139 repeats that row, and line 140 counts every copy in micro-F1.
- experiment.py:165 logs the result as matched_gap.

PROOF AGAINST THE LOGS
I ported sklearn's tree build and depth-first query to stdlib Python, using MSVC's nth_element. One row per stratum reproduces the logged matched_gap exactly on 14 of 14 runs, including 43.27, 37.18, 32.88, 29.43 and 27.82. The matched set is 37 distinct rows, because 2 pairs of the 39 strata share a row. For (4,1), dev id 24 is copied 23 times out of 69 tied rows. My reimplementation of the metrics also matches every logged intent, slot F1 and subgroup F1 value.

CLAIM FIGURES CONFIRMED
- Dev: 215 queries, 39 combinations, maximum multiplicity 23, effective N 17.41, 321 gold slots.
- Test (metadata only, no predictions read): 341 queries, 47 combinations, effective N 17.68.
- Tie-breaks, Stage-1 matched F1: sd 7.89 to 7.99 over three 2,000-draw seeds; 95% range [53.87, 84.14] on 5,000 draws.
- Tie-breaks, change to A1_fresh_lr5e-4: 95% range [-2.61, 21.42] on 20,000 draws. Both ranges agree with the report within Monte Carlo error.
- The reviewer's five all-rows gaps reproduce to 2 decimals if the three no-exact-match queries each use one nearest stratum: (17,1) to (17,2), (16,1) to (15,1), (19,1) to (17,2).
- Selection is unaffected. family_table, best and greedy use dev_joint only (run_ladder.py:59-78, 107), and matched_gap is written only at experiment.py:165.
- Notebook cell 42 has the same flaw, and hand-off section 8 reports its output (also sections 6.2.3, 12.2 and 14).

CORRECTIONS
1. "About 7 points" applies to a wrong-span flip. Stage-1 matched F1 is 77.78 with the (4,1) row right, 73.28 for a plain miss and 70.68 for a wrong span. The real case is a plain miss: id 24 goes from correct under Stage 1 to missed under A1_fresh_lr5e-4. That one row accounts for 4.46 of the logged 13.84 closure, while the fully correct share across all 69 tied rows rises from 58.0% to 73.9%.
2. "Hundreds of exact ties" is overstated. The largest tie sets are 125, 117, 117 and 86, and the median is 12. 98.1% of queries still have more than one tied row.
3. The closure of 0.91 depends on how those three queries are handled. Using all tied rows it is 0.78 with raw distance (gaps 35.68, 37.63, 32.36, 34.89, 28.02) and 1.17 with standardised distance (gaps 36.19, 37.99, 32.51, 35.02, 28.53). The conclusion does not change. The snapshot also dropped cell 42's division by SD, which affects only 3 dev and 5 test queries and at most 0.54 of a gap point.

ADDITIONAL EVIDENCE
- The logged closure is an outlier. Under random tie-breaks the Stage-1 to A1_fresh_lr5e-4 closure has mean 0.77 and 95% range [-12.26, 11.78]. The logged 13.84 sits at the 98.8th percentile, and 42.7% of tie-breaks give a negative closure.
- Stage 1 got a favourable draw. Its picks are all fully correct on the five largest strata (44.7% of queries), so logged matched F1 is 77.78 against 70.19 over all tied rows. That inflates almost every logged closure.
- Three runs change sign with standardised all-ties: A1_ft_recipe +6.09 to -1.79, A2_drop.25 +4.08 to -3.57, A2_ls0 +6.13 to -1.57.
- Matched F1 for Stage 1 to A1_fresh_lr5e-4 moves by -4.68 as logged but by +7.99 over all tied rows.
- Rankings move. Stage 1 has the largest logged gap but ranks 11th of 14 under all-ties. A2_ls.2 goes from 2nd to 5th smallest, and A2_rare1 from 8th to 2nd.
- The value depends on row order. Shuffling the pool rows of the same frame moves the Stage-1 gap across a 95% range of [19.79, 48.66] over 299 shuffles.
- The value may depend on platform. A libstdc++ port gives 36.29 instead of 43.27 on the same frame, so a Colab rerun could log a different number. I did not validate that port against a real run, so treat this as indicative.

SCOPE AND SEVERITY
Major is fair for the reported OOV-gap comparison only. Training, checkpoints, dev_joint, subgroup F1, gain_* and targeted_adv are unaffected. tools/ has no test of matched_control.

One risk goes beyond the claim. run_final_test.py:119-121 (live code, outside the snapshot, read by grep only) computes this metric on test from in-memory frames and has no to_pickle call, so the fix should land before the one-shot test run.

LIMITS OF THIS CHECK
Under the stated limits I ran stdlib Python only, without numpy, pandas or sklearn. Frames were read through inert pickle stubs. Nothing in the project was changed. Scripts are in C:\Users\user\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--Users-user\ef0231a5-9c23-41d4-8ee5-c6ed6580f7ff\scratchpad (mc_step1.py to mc_step7.py, frame_io.py).

votes.reasoning:
The defect is real. I could not refute it, and I confirmed it more directly than the reviewer did. Its reach is limited to the matched-gap number: training, selection and the primary metrics are untouched.

**Mechanism: confirmed**
- With sklearn 1.7.2 source read as text, `algorithm='auto'` resolves to kd_tree with leaf_size 30. The depth-first query keeps the first row found at the minimum distance (`heap_push` returns on `val >= values[0]`). Identical queries therefore always return the same row.
- I ported the tree build and query to pure Python, using my recollection of the MSVC `std::nth_element`. The port reproduces the logged `matched_gap` to 2 decimals on all 13 finished runs.
- Dev: 215 queries, 39 combinations, 37 distinct rows actually used, up to 23 copies. Effective N is 17.41 by combination and 17.38 by actual row, so the reviewer's "at most 39" holds.
- Test metadata: 341 queries, 47 combinations, effective N 17.68, up to 40 copies. No test predictions were read; only the counts in `cache/oov_test.pkl`.
- `tools/smoke.py` does not exercise `matched_control`, and no other code prevents this.

**Concrete failure: same predictions, unchanged estimator**
- Reversing pool row order moves these gaps:

| Run | Logged gap | Reversed order |
|---|---:|---:|
| A1_fresh_lr5e-4 | 29.43 | 41.51 |
| A2_ls.2 | 26.93 | 42.70 |
| A2_drop.25 | 39.19 | 52.65 |
| stage1_baseline | 43.27 | 42.85 |

- Adding cell 42's standardisation, which the snapshot omits, moves Stage 1 from 43.27 to 30.31 and A2_slot2 from 27.82 to 17.86.
- Over 300 random row orders, the Stage-1 gap has mean 35.44, sd 7.54 and 95% range 20.73 to 48.08.
- For A1_fresh_lr5e-4 the closure against Stage 1 has mean 0.55 and 95% range -15.06 to +12.20. The logged 13.84 lies above that range.
- One utterance drives much of this. Dev id 24 (gold `O O B-house_place O`) is the (4,1) pick, copied 23 times. It is right in Stage 1 and A2_rare1 and wrong in the other 11 runs.
- That single row explains 4.46 of A1_fresh_lr5e-4's 4.68-point fall in matched F1. It shifts 11 of the 12 Stage-1-relative closures by about 4.5 points.
- The contradiction shows without any simulation. No-Train-OOV F1 rose from 71.51 to 79.00, while the matched subset of that same pool fell from 77.78 to 73.10.

**Size of the effect (my all-rows recomputation, raw distance)**

| Run | Logged gap | All-rows gap | Raw group gap |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| stage1_baseline | 43.27 | 35.68 | 37.00 |
| A1_ft_recipe | 37.18 | 37.63 | 38.17 |
| A1_fresh_recipe | 32.88 | 32.36 | 32.76 |
| A1_fresh_lr5e-4 | 29.43 | 34.89 | 35.33 |
| A2_slot2 | 27.82 | 28.02 | 28.66 |

- A1_fresh_lr5e-4 closure is 13.84 logged, against 0.78 all-rows, 1.17 with standardised distance and 1.67 on the raw group gap.
- Closure changes sign on three runs (logged vs all-rows): A1_ft_recipe +6.09 vs -1.95, A2_drop.25 +4.08 vs -3.89, A2_ls0 +6.13 vs -1.90.
- The comparison between Stage-2 methods also reverses. Logged gaps put A2_slot2 (27.82) ahead of A2_rare1 (32.98); all-rows puts A2_rare1 (26.68) ahead of A2_slot2 (28.02).
- The logged Stage-1 gap suggests that controlling for difficulty widens the gap (43.27 vs raw 37.00). All-rows says it narrows it (35.68).

**Corrections to the report (none changes the conclusion)**
- Their all-rows gaps differ from mine by at most 0.33 (35.49 vs 35.68, 34.58 vs 34.89, 27.69 vs 28.02). I tried several variants and could not identify theirs exactly.
- "About 7 points" for a (4,1) flip is the upper case. From Stage-1 counts TP 252, FP 72, FN 72, a missed slot gives 73.28 (-4.50) and a wrong span gives 70.68 (-7.10). The flip seen between Stage 1 and A1_fresh_lr5e-4 is the missed-slot kind.
- Their simulations reproduce: Stage-1 sd 7.71 and range 54.08 to 84.12 (theirs 7.78, 53.91 to 83.70); Stage 1 to A1_fresh_lr5e-4 change -2.79 to +21.58 (theirs -2.35 to +21.27).
- "Hundreds of exact ties" is loose: 1,061 tied rows across 39 cells, largest cell 125, median 12.

**What limits it**
- Selection is unaffected. `family_table` (`run_ladder.py` lines 59-67) aggregates only `dev_joint`, `dev_intent`, `dev_slot_f1` and `params_total`.
- `matched_gap` reaches only `dev_metrics.json` and `leaderboard.csv`.
- `matched_control` is also called by `run_final_test.py:119` and `build_notebook.py:277`, so a single-row value would appear in `matched_control_test.csv` and `main.ipynb`.
- Intent accuracy, slot F1, subgroup F1 and the bootstrap do not use it, and no retraining is needed.
- "Major" is therefore fair for any report sentence built on the matched gap, but not for the ladder's outcome.
- Cell 42 has the same flaw (`n_neighbors=1`). So hand-off sections 6.2.3, 8, 12.2 and 14 rest on single-row picks too, and agreeing with the reference does not make it correct.

**How this was checked**

- The scripts are stdlib-only and read the pickles through inert stubs; no project file was changed.

votes.better_fix:
Adopt the reviewer's all-tied-rows fix. Replace the body of `matched_control` in `src/evaluate.py` and delete the sklearn import on line 7; nothing else in the file uses it.

```python
def matched_control(merged):
    """No-Train-OOV slot F1 reweighted to the Slot-Train-OOV mix of (length, #slots). Each query uses ALL pool
    rows at its minimum standardised distance, each weighted 1/k, so row order cannot change the result."""
    slot = merged[merged["train_oov_group"] == "Slot-Train-OOV"]
    pool = merged[merged["train_oov_group"] == "No-Train-OOV"]
    feats = ["n_tokens", "n_gold_slots"]
    Xs, Xp = slot[feats].to_numpy(float), pool[feats].to_numpy(float)
    sd = np.vstack([Xs, Xp]).std(0)
    sd[sd == 0] = 1.0
    c = np.array([slot_counts([g], [p]) for g, p in zip(pool["gold_tags"], pool["pred_tags"])], float)
    tot = np.zeros(3)
    for q in Xs:
        d = (((Xp - q) / sd) ** 2).sum(1)
        tot += c[d <= d.min() + 1e-9].mean(0)
    tp, fp, fn = tot
    f_m = 100.0 * 2 * tp / max(2 * tp + fp + fn, 1e-9)
    f_s = metrics_from_frame(slot)["slot_micro_f1"]
    return {"matched_no_oov_f1": f_m, "slot_oov_f1": f_s, "gap": f_m - f_s,
            "avg_tokens": float(slot["n_tokens"].mean()), "avg_slots": float(slot["n_gold_slots"].mean())}
```

**Standardising:** this follows cell 42, which the snapshot currently omits. The choice is now minor: only 3 dev and 5 test queries lack an exact cell, and raw and standardised gaps differ by at most 0.54 across the 13 runs.

**Check after implementing:** on the current frames this should give about 36.19 for stage1_baseline, 37.99 for A1_ft_recipe, 32.51 for A1_fresh_recipe, 35.02 for A1_fresh_lr5e-4 and 28.53 for A2_slot2. Also add a smoke assertion that shuffling the frame's rows leaves the gap unchanged (absolute difference below 1e-9).

**Recompute old values:**
- `run()` returns early for finished runs (`experiment.py` lines 111-117), so existing JSON files will not update on their own.
- For every `results/*/dev_pred_frame.pkl`, write `matched_control(pd.read_pickle(p))["gap"]`, rounded to 2 decimals, into `matched_gap` in that run's `dev_metrics.json`. Then call `rebuild_leaderboard()`.
- Do this after the current ladder finishes. The running process keeps the old function, and selection does not read this field, so there is no reason to interrupt it.
- Never mix old and new values on one leaderboard.

**Reporting:** do not compare the new values with the hand-off's 39.00 and 26.84, which came from single-row picks.

findings.title: greedy() combines variants that the code forbids, which crashes rungs C and R on every restart
findings.claim: greedy() only skips variants that share a config field name (lines 97-99). Two forbidden pairs use different field names, so they pass that check. slot_head=biaffine with factorized, slot_to_intent or intent_to_slot fails the assert at src/models.py:335. adv_eps with sam_rho fails the assert at src/train.py:139. The AssertionError is not caught by run() (RuntimeError only) or by __main__ (ResourceAbort only).
findings.failure_scenario: Rung C: results are sorted best first, and biaffine and factorized both beat base_score. Step 0 sets cur to base+biaffine. Line 105 then derives C2g2_factorized with slot_head=biaffine and factorized=True, build_model raises AssertionError, and the process exits with a traceback. The reverse order fails the same way, and i2s or s2i can stand in for factorized. Rung R: adv.05 and sam.05 both beat base_score; cur holds one, the derived config has adv_eps>0 and sam_rho>0, and train_model asserts at line 139. Finished runs replay with identical values, so each restart hits the same line. confirm() and the rung table are never reached, and in rung R neither is R3. Downstream, the rung's variants stay at n=1. If the operator moves on, best('ABC', min_seeds=3) and best('ABCDR', min_seeds=3) silently ignore that rung's results, because they only accept families with 3 seeds.
findings.suggested_fix: Add explicit conflict groups to greedy(): {adv_eps, sam_rho} and biaffine vs {factorized, slot_to_intent, intent_to_slot}. Alternatively, catch AssertionError around execute() in greedy and treat the candidate as dropped, printing the reason.

Replace run_ladder.py lines 137 to 142 so the base comes only from the values `execute` returns for the three A1 candidates, not from the leaderboard:

```python
def rung_A(ctx):
    s1 = ModelConfig()
    a1 = (Cand("A1_ft_recipe", s1, TrainConfig(lr=1e-4, **RECIPE), "stage1"),
          Cand("A1_fresh_recipe", s1, TrainConfig(lr=3e-4, **RECIPE)),
          Cand("A1_fresh_lr5e-4", s1, TrainConfig(lr=5e-4, **RECIPE)))
    note = "recipe: 40 epochs, cosine, warm-up, label smoothing .1, word dropout .1"
    # Base from these seed-42 rows only, so a restart rebuilds identical A2 configs.
    joints = [execute(ctx, c, "A", note=note)["dev_joint"] for c in a1]
    score = max(joints)
    base = a1[joints.index(score)]
    print(f"BASE <- {base.name}: joint {score:.2f}", flush=True)
```

**Why this works:** on a restart, `execute` returns the stored row for each A1 run, and those three seed-42 rows do not change. A2 and A3 rows and confirm seeds therefore cannot move the base. The exact-rung filter can still be moved by confirm seeds.

**Check on today's rows:** joints are [78.64, 78.6, 79.1], so the base is A1_fresh_lr5e-4 at 79.1, matching log line 140. Its config equals the stored A1 row, and the replay gives _same_config True for A2_drop.10. Finished A2 rows should therefore be reported as already done, so no results need migrating.

**What it leaves unchanged:** line 161 can still confirm an extra family on a restart, but that only adds rows and overwrites nothing. Line 177 in rung B is not changed by this fix.

**Timing:** apply this before any restart of rung A. The running job keeps the code it already loaded, so the fix takes effect on the next start.

reviews.coverage_notes:
METHOD: Traced the code by reading it. I ran no torch, sklearn or sentencepiece, and only tiny stdlib scripts (parameter sums, cumulative LR, reading notebook cells). I also read results/*/dev_metrics.json, three history.csv files and cache/emb_stats.json from the live project, read-only, as evidence. These were written by the running job, so they reflect the live code, not necessarily the snapshot.

CHECKED AND FOUND CORRECT
- Stage-1 against cells 22 and 30: same modules, order and padding-mask polarity (~mask), masked mean pooling, plain CE with ignore_index -100, AdamW 3e-4 / wd 1e-4 (two param groups at the same LR), clip 1.0 over all trainable params, same dev-joint selection and patience logic. Differences that do not change the method: a seeded shuffle generator, and enable_nested_tensor=False, which has no effect with norm_first=True.
- Adapters against cells 51, 55 and 57: same sizes, same masked mean, same h[-2]/h[-1] composition, residual added before positional encoding. Zero-initialised parts still receive gradient after the first step.
- Frozen rows and swap path: index offsets, torch.where gating (no spurious gradient to the clamped base row), PCA inverse-map shapes, row reordering after the memmap read.
- BiLSTM and pre_lstm: packing, total_length, unsorting, hidden sizes, zero residual.
- Attention pooling and label attention: pads masked before softmax, softmax over the right dimension, zero query equals mean pooling up to float rounding.
- hier_intent: indexing and scenario targets. i2s/s2i: order, broadcasting, O column dropped under both schemes.
- Factorized head: prefix and type indexing under BIO and BIOES.
- CRF: pad handling in the gold score and partition, start/end masks, BIOES end constraints, per-token normalisation, Viterbi history indexing. BIO and BIOES constraint matrices.
- Biaffine: start/end axes, triu on the last two dims, smoothing with reduction=sum, token normalisation, greedy non-overlap decode, BIO output.
- Token-intent loss: _h_tok[mask] row-major order matches repeat_interleave. aux_lm: targets are original base ids, always below V in train data.
- corrupt_batch: rate formula, O=0 under both schemes, -100 excluded, only lexical non-pad tokens touched, swap only where a row exists, no in-place mutation of cached rows.
- Schedule: warm-up and cosine are computed from len(train_loader) and tc.epochs, so total_steps stays right for bs32 and ep80. Scheduler stepped after opt.step. The emb_lr_mult group scales correctly and frozen tables are excluded from the optimiser.
- EMA: buffers copied, dev run on the shadow, best state saved from the shadow, live weights restored before continuing.
- Adversarial: gradient captured on the pre-delta embedding, sign, per-utterance scale, mask, gradients accumulated with the clean pass. With R-Drop it uses the second pass's embedding, which is still valid.
- R-Drop: KL direction, batchmean over utterances and over tokens, _scen_logits and _h_tok read before the next forward. SAM: perturb, zero, second pass, restore, then clip, step, scheduler, EMA.
- Early stopping, patience, checkpoint contents (plain types, safe under weights_only=True). State leaks: mention_replace is reset in finally, _track_emb and _emb cannot leak between runs, _tok is per dataset.
- Metric matches cell 26. Scenario names, device placement of buffers, indices and lengths, and the _same_config JSON round trip are correct. On disk, A1_ft_recipe epoch 0 equals Stage 1 (82.83 / 66.09).

CAVEATS, NOT REPORTED AS DEFECTS
- CRF transitions start at 0 and share the base LR. Cumulative LR over 40 epochs is 1.80 at lr 5e-4, the current A1 best, but only 0.36 at lr 1e-4, so soft transitions would be weak on a 1e-4 base.
- s2i input is divided by utterance length. A one-token slot in a 7-token utterance gives 0.14, so the logit shift is bounded near 0.26 per channel at lr 5e-4. Weak but not a no-op.
- The biaffine slot loss is a sum over spans per token. It starts about 16 times the intent loss, then falls to a label-smoothing floor near 0.7 per span, roughly 3 per token, which carries no gradient. I found no concrete unfairness, but lambda_slot is not retuned for it.
- dev_loss is not comparable across heads. CRF and biaffine use their own slot loss, and hier adds its scenario term despite the 'plain joint loss' docstring. It is not used for selection and only affects logs and curves.
- CRF has no slot label smoothing. The R-Drop slot KL is skipped for biaffine by design.
- A1_ft_recipe started exactly at Stage 1, but the current A1 best is fresh, so the epoch-0 assert at src/experiment.py line 172 does not apply to fresh-based descendants.

COULD NOT CHECK
- Anything needing a GPU run. In particular, known cuDNN RNN non-determinism could flip one prediction and trip the 1e-6 re-evaluation assert at src/experiment.py line 170 for char, pre_lstm or bilstm runs, which would discard the finished run before metrics are written. Transformer runs have passed it so far.
- VRAM use for biaffine and BIOES CRF. My estimate is under 1 GB at T=61.
- Actual emission margins behind the CRF and s2i caveats.
- The attn e0 float-rounding flip risk I estimated at about 1e-3 or less, not measured.

OUT OF MY LENS, NOTED ONLY
- metrics_path.write_text is not atomic, so a truncated dev_metrics.json after an unclean reboot would make rebuild_leaderboard raise until the file is removed.
- The run_ladder.py docstring advertises rung E, but RUNGS has no E, so it would raise KeyError. The snapshot also has no test-evaluation path.
- The BIO label inventory is built from all splits, matching notebook cell 10.

findings.title: Greedy compares seed-42 variants against a 3-seed base mean
findings.claim: In rungs C and R, base_score is the family mean over 3 seeds returned by best(..., min_seeds=3) (lines 197 and 240, passed at lines 216 and 251). Each screened joint score comes from a single seed-42 run. The base family was selected partly on its seed-42 score, so that score is biased above the mean and the bar is too low. The top variant is then adopted at lines 100-103 with no paired comparison against the base's own seed-42 run.
findings.failure_scenario: Base seeds score 78.20 (seed 42), 77.70 and 77.60, so the mean is 77.83. A variant scoring 77.90 at seed 42 is 0.30 worse than the base on the same seed, yet it passes line 95. If it is the top result it becomes cur, score is reset to 77.90, and later variants stack on a configuration that did not improve the base. A real variant can then be tested on the wrong starting point or dropped. The low bar also makes the two greedy crash combinations more likely. The final 3-seed selection limits the damage, but the greedy families reported are affected.
findings.suggested_fix: Compare against the base's seed-42 dev_joint, taken from the row that best() already reads, and return that value for use in greedy.

Refuted as a defect. The mechanics in the report are accurate, but the conclusion that the bar is too low does not follow, the harm is very small, and the suggested fix should not be applied. Line numbers without a file refer to C:/Users/user/massive_joint_nlu/.review_snapshot/run_ladder.py.

WHAT IS TRUE
- best() returns the family mean at line 78, and lines 197/216 and 240/251 pass it to greedy.
- The base row is the seed-42 row (line 75), so every screened run also uses seed 42.
- With 78.20, 77.70 and 77.60 the bar is 77.8333. So 77.90 passes line 95, and lines 100-103 set cur and score = 77.90.
- I ran the snapshot's greedy function with stubs. The current bar adopts the variant and runs later stacks; a 78.20 bar does nothing.
- The selection bias exists: top_names orders unconfirmed families by their one seed-42 score.

WHY THE CONCLUSION FAILS
1. That bias makes the base's seed-42 score the inflated number, not the mean.
- Seeds 7 and 1234 were drawn after selection, and both landed at least 0.50 below 78.20. The variant's 77.90 beats two of the three base runs.
- These numbers cannot separate "the variant is worse" from "the base got lucky at seed 42", and they lean towards the second.
- Mirror case on the same numbers: if the base's true level is about 77.65, two real +0.25 variants would score about 77.90 and 77.88. A 78.20 bar blocks both, so their stack never runs.

2. A same-seed comparison only wins if same-seed runs share most of their noise.
- With same-seed correlation r, it has lower variance than the mean comparison only when r > 1/2: 2(1-r) against 4/3 - 2r/3, in units of the noise variance.
- It has smaller selection bias only when r > 2/3: (1-r) against |r-1/3|, times the inflation.
- Pairing is real but partial. src/train.py:140 reseeds after the model build, and src/train.py:20-21 seed the shuffle.

3. The harm is limited.
- greedy's return value is discarded at lines 160, 216 and 251.
- Screen rows stay on the leaderboard, so a variant dropped from the stack still competes in top_names.
- best(..., min_seeds=3) then compares 3-seed means, including the base's own.
- The only effect is which stack runs exist: at most 3 per rung (2 in R). A2 runs took about 150 to 190 s; CRF or biaffine stacks may take longer.

- The true gain of the final pick differed by at most 0.06 points between the bars.

- In the mostly-null rung the gap was at most 0.001. There the suggested bar adopted a truly worse top variant up to 8 percentage points less often, without changing the final pick.

findings.title: OOM retry keeps its own reserved VRAM, so the guard can stall and then stop instead of retrying
findings.claim: torch.cuda.empty_cache() runs inside the except block, while e.__traceback__ still pins the train_model frames holding the model, optimiser and batch tensors. `del model` removes only run()'s reference, so nothing is released, including during the 5-minute sleep. Those tensors are freed only when the except block ends, and they go back to PyTorch's cache, which stays reserved. The next attempt calls guard.check(need_vram=True) at src/train.py line 141 before anything else clears the cache. nvidia-smi counts that reserved memory as used (src/guard.py lines 33-34 and 49).
findings.failure_scenario: The other GPU job holds most of the VRAM and this process has about 1.7 GB reserved when it hits OOM. On the retry, nvidia-smi reports under 1500 MB free even though this process could reuse its own cache. The guard pauses for up to MAX_WAIT_S, one hour, then raises ResourceAbort and the ladder exits with 'STOPPED SAFELY'. The intended 4-attempt retry never trains again unless the other job frees memory. No results are lost, but the unattended run stops early.
findings.suggested_fix: After leaving the except block and before the next attempt, call gc.collect() and then torch.cuda.empty_cache(), or sleep and clear the cache after the block.

votes.reasoning:
Not refuted. The defect is real and "minor" is the right severity, but the harm is narrower than the failure scenario suggests.

**Code trace (snapshot line numbers)**
1. An OOM inside train_model is caught at experiment.py:139. While `e` is bound, e.__traceback__ holds the train_model and _train_step frames. Their locals include model (the same object as run()'s, because .to() returns self at train.py:144), opt, ema, counts, b and loss.
2. Line 143 `del model` drops only run()'s name.
3. Line 144 empty_cache() can only release unoccupied blocks. The installed torch 1.13.1 docstring (cuda/memory.py:114-116) says it "Releases all unoccupied cached memory" so that it becomes "visible in nvidia-smi".
4. Line 145 then sleeps 300 s with all of that memory still allocated.
5. When the except block ends, Python deletes `e`, the frames die and the tensors return to the cache. Reserved memory does not change.
6. The next attempt runs seed_everything (config.py:37-42), build_model (CPU only, models.py:493-499) and, for warm starts, torch.load(map_location="cpu"). It then reaches guard.check(need_vram=True) at train.py:141.
7. The only empty_cache calls in the snapshot are experiment.py:144 and 191, so nothing clears the cache first. need_vram=True also bypasses the throttle (guard.py:58).
8. guard.py:33-34 returns total minus used, and used includes this process's reserved memory. guard.py:49 then adds the "free VRAM" reason.
9. The wait loop at guard.py:66-70 clears nothing and raises ResourceAbort at line 68 after 3600 s. experiment.py:140 re-raises it, and run_ladder.py:280-282 prints STOPPED SAFELY and exits with code 3.

**Check I ran**
I executed the real guard.py source and the real experiment.py lines 127-145 with stubs for nvidia-smi, the clock and the allocator. It was stdlib only and wrote no files. The values were total 8188 MB, other use 6400 MB, and an attempt needing 1900 MB, which hits OOM at 1700 MB reserved.
- **Current code, other job stable:** line 144 leaves reserved at 1700 -> 1700 with 1700 still allocated, and the same holds during the sleep. At the retry, allocated is 0 and reserved is 1700. The guard reports "free VRAM 88 MB" and raises ResourceAbort at t=3930 s.
- **Other job frees 300 MB during the sleep:** the current code sees 388 MB and aborts at t=3930 s. With the fix below it sees 2088 MB and the run completes at t=300 s.
- **Other job frees 1500 MB at t=1000:** the current code resumes and completes at t=1020 s, which matches the report's "unless the other job frees memory".

The allocator and nvidia-smi are modelled from torch's documented behaviour. Nothing ran on the GPU, as the limits require.

**Where the report overstates**
- Let F be the free VRAM with this process's cache empty, and R its reserved memory at OOM. The bug changes the outcome only when F >= 1500 and F - R < 1500.
- With a stable other job, OOM implies R is about F and at least 1500 MB, so only heavy variants can reach this case. The Stage-1-sized model has 4.34M parameters (ladder_A.log), and I estimate it reserves a few hundred MB. That is not measured, and the logs record no VRAM figures.
- If the other job grew instead, F is about R and below 1500 right after the OOM. The guard blocks with or without a fix, and the bug only means the other job must give back R more.
- With a stable other job and the same seed and memory demand, a retry OOMs again. In the stub with the fix, that gave three more OOMs and a plain RuntimeError at t=900 s. run_ladder.py catches only ResourceAbort, so that ends in a traceback rather than STOPPED SAFELY.
- So the real harm is the partial-easing case, where the other job frees a little, not the stable case in the report. No results are lost either way, and finished runs are skipped on restart.
- Grepping results/*.log and *.txt found no [guard] or out-of-memory lines, so this path has not fired yet.

Besides the snapshot, I read those logs (read-only) and the installed torch sources.
votes.better_fix:
In src/experiment.py, add `import gc` and move lines 143-145 out of the except block, so the cleanup runs after `e` and its traceback are gone:

```python
        try:
            model, ckpt = train_model(model, ctx.assets, ds["train"], ds["dev"], tcfg, name, meta=meta, verbose=verbose)
            break
        except RuntimeError as e:
            if isinstance(e, guard.ResourceAbort) or "out of memory" not in str(e).lower() or attempt == 3:
                raise
            print(f"[{name}] GPU out of memory, waiting 5 minutes before retry {attempt + 1}", flush=True)
        # Outside the except block: the traceback no longer pins the failed attempt's frames.
        del model
        gc.collect()
        torch.cuda.empty_cache()
        time.sleep(300)
```

- **Why this path is safe:** the new lines run only on a retryable OOM, because `break` and `raise` both skip them. `del model` must stay, because run() still holds the failed model at that point.
- **Why not the report's second option:** sleeping in the block and clearing afterwards would keep the VRAM held during the 5-minute wait. Freeing first gives that memory back to the other job while this one waits.
- **Separate optional change:** the final OOM at line 140 raises a plain RuntimeError, which run_ladder.py does not catch. Raising `guard.ResourceAbort(...) from e` there would keep the "STOPPED SAFELY" exit when the other job never eases.

reviews.coverage_notes:
METHOD AND SCOPE. I reviewed the snapshot by reading and tracing only. No torch, sklearn or sentencepiece was imported and no training was started. Nothing in the project was modified.
I also ran tiny stdlib Python scripts that called nvidia-smi and tasklist. That goes slightly beyond "Read, Grep and Glob", though both are small read-only queries.
For live evidence I read files outside the snapshot: results/ladder_A.log, stage1_log.txt, dev_metrics.json files, keep_awake.txt, tools/keep_awake.py and the first 30 lines of live src/guard.py. All findings cite snapshot lines.

CHECKED AND FOUND CORRECT
- Dev-only selection: train_model, best, top_names and greedy all use dev scores.
- Test isolation: no snapshot path evaluates a model on test. Context touches test only for load assertions, the label inventory and OOV metadata. Measured non-O labels: train 106, dev 96, test 100, union 107. Only I-transport_type comes solely from test. This inherited extra output has no selection effect.
- JSON round trips: flagged, k_extra and seed keep usable types. The legacy Stage-1 row is handled by setdefault, and its NaN frozen_dim is safe because it is filtered out by rung.
- row_to_cand round trip is correct, including frozen_dim, n_frozen and a recomputed flagged. run() re-applies n_frozen.
- _same_config: list/tuple and float round trips are fine. It ignores init, but I found no ladder path where only init differs.
- Half-finished runs (checkpoint without metrics) are retrained correctly.
- Determinism between attempts: reseeding at experiment.py:128 and train.py:140 plus a new loader generator make attempts repeatable.
- screen compares like with like. The first greedy variant is applied correctly. The name A3_<key> never runs and appears only in later notes (cosmetic).
- confirm picks the seed-42 row and builds correct names and rung labels. diff_config is dead code in the snapshot.
- derive handles init=None and k correctly, including dict(fresh, m=..., t=...) in rung D.
- All override field names are valid. I found no name collisions on a first pass, and a variant identical to its base is harmless.
- Rung D's largest realistic config is about 16.3M parameters, under the cap.
- min_seeds=3 finds a family whenever the earlier rung's confirm ran. Otherwise it raises IndexError, or silently ignores the unconfirmed rung if that rung's confirm never ran (see the R2 and C2 findings).

GUARD AND ASSERTIONS
- Epoch-0 assertion: the log shows A1_ft_recipe at exactly 82.83/66.09. Every warm-start switch adds an exact zero except attn pooling, whose rounding could flip an argmax only with negligible probability.
- Re-evaluation assertion: it has passed on all finished Transformer runs, including every A1 and A2 run so far.
- No pause path can hang: nvidia-smi has a timeout and parse errors are caught. An abort loses only the current run (about 3 minutes), apart from the rung A base change.
- RAM: 2344 MB available when sampled, and process peak is stable at about 2.79 GB. I estimate ext150k_pca100 adds about 390 MB at guard checks, giving about 1.1 GB from a 1.5 GB baseline, above the 900 MB limit. That margin is thin.
- VRAM: RTX 4060 Laptop, 8188 MiB total, about 1150 used, so MIN_FREE_VRAM_MB only matters if another application fills the card.
- Temperature: 17 samples during rung A ranged 78-88 C, with SW thermal slowdown often Active, and the log has no [guard] lines yet. MAX_TEMP_C=86 sits inside that range, so occasional pauses are expected. They cost wall-clock time only.
- Disk: 17.6 MB per checkpoint, 0.34 MB per prediction frame, about 3 GB estimated for roughly 110 runs, 80 GB free. No risk.
- OOM message matching and ResourceAbort passthrough are correct. An OOM in the post-training predict at experiment.py:148 is outside the retry, but the window is very small.

NOT DEFECTS BUT WORTH KNOWING
- The 3-seed mean includes the screened seed-42 run, so families from larger screens get a slightly inflated mean (about +0.6 sigma for the best of 15 noise draws). This is a design limit, not a bug.
- _same_config has no notion of code version. After fixes that change training behaviour, finished runs still count as already done and are silently reused, so decide explicitly which results to invalidate.
- Live state: file ages suggest the running rung A process matches the snapshot, and live run_ladder.py and guard.py were edited after it started. Avoid restarting rung A until the base-change finding is fixed.

COULD NOT CHECK
- GPU behaviour, because nothing could be run. In particular, the 1e-6 re-evaluation assert has not yet been exercised on CUDA LSTMs (char adapter, pre_lstm, bilstm). PyTorch documents possible non-determinism there, and one flipped token would stop the rung with an AssertionError. Check the first B1_char run.
- Real cool-down time from 86 to 76 C.
- run_final_test.py, src/posthoc.py, build_notebook.py and live rung_E are outside the snapshot, so "test evaluated once at the end" is confirmed only for snapshot code.
- Interaction with tools/keep_awake.py (also outside the snapshot, not reviewed in depth): it exits after 30 minutes without log writes, while a guard pause can stay silent for up to 60 minutes, so idle sleep could then suspend the ladder.

findings.title: Greedy compares seed-42 variants with the base's 3-seed mean
findings.claim: In rungs C and R, base_score is the family mean returned by best(..., min_seeds=3) (lines 78, 197, 240), while `joint` is a single seed-42 run on the base's seed-42 configuration. The filter and the unconditional step-0 acceptance at line 101 therefore compare unlike quantities. Because the base reached confirmation on its seed-42 rank, its seed-42 score usually exceeds its mean, so the filter is biased toward accepting variants. Later greedy steps do compare like with like.
findings.failure_scenario: Base seeds 42/7/1234 = 80.40/79.90/79.90, mean 80.07. C1_i2s at seed 42 = 80.20 is 0.20 worse than the same-seed base but passes 80.20 > 80.07. If it ranks first, cur becomes base+i2s and all later greedy runs build on a configuration that lost like for like. The opposite case also occurs: base seeds 79.6/80.2/80.2, mean 80.0, and a variant at 79.9 (+0.3 at the same seed) is dropped. The final 3-seed selection limits the damage, but greedy explores different combinations, and the looser filter raises the chance of the R2 and C2 crashes.
findings.suggested_fix: Have best() also return the base's seed-42 dev_joint and pass that to greedy(). Keep the mean for reporting only.

votes.reasoning:
Refuted as a defect, not as a description. The control flow and arithmetic are exactly as reported, but the conclusion that this is wrong does not hold up, and the proposed fix is not clearly better.

CONFIRMED FROM THE CODE
- best() takes r from the seed-42 row (run_ladder.py:75) but returns the family mean (:78).
- screen() derives from that row, so variants keep seed 42 (:85). Line 95 compares the two values, and line 101 accepts the top variant that passes.
- I ran the real greedy body, extracted with ast, using stubbed execute and derive:
  - Seeds 80.40/79.90/79.90: the mean is 80.0667, i2s at 80.20 is accepted and C2g2_attn runs. With 80.40 as the bar, nothing runs.
  - Seeds 79.6/80.2/80.2: a variant at 79.90 is dropped. With 79.60 as the bar, it is accepted.
- Rung A compares same-seed scores on a first pass (ladder_A.log:141, "over 1 seed(s)"), so the comparator does differ between rungs.

WHY THAT IS NOT WRONG BEHAVIOUR
1. Bias. The base's seed-42 score is the inflated number, because that is the score it was selected on. The mean is less inflated.
   - A fresh variant draw compared with the mean is biased toward accepting only if the variant inherits much of the base's seed-42 luck. The threshold is a correlation above 1/3 analytically, and about 0.67 in simulation once best()'s selection on the mean is included.
   - At zero correlation the simulated bias is -0.14 against the mean and -0.21 against seed 42, so the proposed bar is the more biased one.
   - "Usually exceeds" does hold, but modestly: 62% of the time, by +0.07 on average in simulation.
   - Per-variant decision accuracy (mean bar vs seed-42 bar) is 71.0 vs 68.7 at correlation 0, 72.9 vs 73.3 at 0.5, and 75.5 vs 84.8 at 0.9.
   - The code cannot settle that correlation. Same-seed runs share batch order and usually the dropout stream (train.py:140, make_loaders), but chaotic divergence over thousands of steps is unmeasured, and only seed-42 runs exist so far.
   - Later greedy steps are not bias-free either: they compare against the top of a sorted screen, which is itself a selected draw.
2. Consequence. greedy's return value is discarded (:160, :216, :251). It only adds runs to the leaderboard, and selection is on 3-seed means in best(), so no reported number or selection rule is invalidated.
   - Because results are sorted, the higher bar's runs were a prefix of the lower bar's on 10,000/10,000 random lists. The looser bar explores the same combinations plus a few more, not different ones.
   - In a full-rung simulation across 6 noise settings, the selected model's true score favoured the current code by 0.003 to 0.06 at correlation up to 0.5, and favoured the fix by 0.006 to 0.03 at 0.9. Simulation error is about 0.006, and assumed seed noise is 0.2 to 0.4.
   - The looser bar usually costs 0.1 to 0.5 extra runs per rung at correlation up to 0.5, about 3 minutes each for the plain configurations logged so far.
   - These figures come from a model with assumed noise, not from training runs.
3. Crashes. The looser bar does reach them more often, but they exist under either bar and are the real risk.
   - With adv.05 and sam.05 both passing, R2g2_sam.05 reached execute with adv_eps and sam_rho both set under both bars, which trips the train.py:139 assert.
   - By reading models.py:335, biaffine combined with factorized, i2s or s2i trips an assert there.
   - Neither AssertionError is caught (experiment.py:139, run_ladder.py:280). They need a direct fix, because changing the comparator leaves them in place.

Why confidence is medium: the mechanics are certain, but the judgement that this is harmless rests on simulation assumptions and an unmeasured same-seed correlation.

On a first pass all candidates have n=1, but after any partial or finished confirm, confirmed families have regressed toward their true mean and compare against unconfirmed n=1 scores.     lb = rebuild_leaderboard()

findings.title: Guard resume requires 76 C even when heat was not the cause
findings.claim: The wait loop always calls _reasons(need_vram, cooling=True), so every pause, including one caused only by RAM or VRAM, can end only at GPU temperature <= RESUME_TEMP_C. That is stricter than the 86 C limit under which training was allowed to run. Idle cooling normally clears this, but another load on the GPU does not.
findings.failure_scenario: A second GPU process keeps the card at 80 C. Available RAM dips to 850 MB at an epoch end, causing "pausing (low RAM 850 MB)". RAM recovers to 1.5 GB a minute later, but 80 > 76 keeps the loop waiting. After 3600 s, ResourceAbort reports "still unsafe (GPU 80C)", the ladder exits with code 3, the current run is lost and nothing restarts it. In rung A the restart also triggers the base change. The same happens for a VRAM pause at run start.
findings.suggested_fix: Use the cooling limit only if temperature was among the reasons when the pause began. Otherwise keep comparing against MAX_TEMP_C while waiting for RAM or VRAM.

votes.reasoning:
The defect is real, and "minor" is the right severity.

Trace with the reported values (card at 80 C, RAM 850 MB, then 1500 MB):
1. train.py:241 calls guard.check(run_name). need_vram is False. The call is not throttled if 20 s have passed since the last check.
2. guard.py:61 calls _reasons(False, cooling=False). 850 < 900 adds "low RAM 850 MB". The limit is 86 and 80 >= 86 is false, so there is no GPU reason. Line 65 prints "pausing (low RAM 850 MB)".
3. guard.py:70 hard-codes cooling=True. RAM at 1500 MB clears, but the limit is now 76 and 80 > 76, so reasons becomes ["GPU 80C"]. The loop continues at a temperature the entry check had just accepted.
4. guard.py:67-68 raises ResourceAbort on the first poll after 3600 s.
5. The exception passes through the try/finally at train.py:206-243, is re-raised at experiment.py:139-141, and run_ladder.py:280-282 prints STOPPED SAFELY and exits with code 3.
6. On restart, experiment.py:111 needs dev_metrics.json, which is only written at line 185 after training finishes, so the run retrains from epoch 0. The project has no .ps1, .bat, .cmd or .sh wrapper that would restart it.

Simulation: I executed the real guard.py source with fake psutil, subprocess and time on a virtual clock, in memory only, with nothing written to the project.
- This scenario aborted at t=3630 s with "RUN: still unsafe after 3600s (GPU 80C)".
- The VRAM variant (train.py:141, need_vram=True, free VRAM 1000 then 3000 MB, 80 C) aborted the same way.

The "working as designed" defence does not hold. The docstring promises a stop only if "the condition does not clear". Here the condition did clear, and the same 80 C was acceptable while training ran. The smoke test has no guard coverage.

What limits the impact:
- It needs a foreign GPU load holding the card at 77-85 C for the whole hour. Without one the card idles down and the only cost is a longer pause (simulated: 600 s instead of 60 s).
- results/ladder_A.log has no [guard] line so far, so this has not fired.
- The lost run is cheap: stored metrics show about 100-190 s per run. The real cost is a one-hour stall, then a ladder that stays stopped.
- The VRAM variant is narrower: the other process must release VRAM yet keep the card hot.
- The claim's "can end only at <= 76 C" has one exception. _gpu() returns (None, None) on any nvidia-smi failure, so a single failed poll skips the temperature test. This does not refute the claim.

The rung A sub-claim holds on current results. Log line 141 shows base A1_fresh_lr5e-4 at 79.10, and results now contain A2_rare1 at 79.73. A restart's best("A") at run_ladder.py:142 would pick A2_rare1, and screen() would then retrain the other A2_ variants because their configuration no longer matches. This fires on any rung A restart once a finished A2 run beats A1. It is a separate defect in run_ladder.py, and the guard fix does not remove it.

Not verified: real card temperatures under a foreign load. I did not query the hardware, per the task limits; only the presence of nvidia-smi.exe was confirmed. The trigger temperatures are the claim's scenario values.

Latch the cooling state in check(), replacing the wait loop at guard.py:66-70. Nothing else changes.

    cooling = False
    while reasons:
        if time.time() - start > MAX_WAIT_S:
            raise ResourceAbort(f"{tag}: still unsafe after {MAX_WAIT_S}s ({', '.join(reasons)})")
        cooling = cooling or any(r.startswith("GPU") for r in reasons)

- VRAM pause at 80 C: resumes at 60 s.
- Heat pause 88 C, then steady 80 C: still aborts at 3630 s, as designed.

findings.title: GPU OOM cleanup runs while the traceback still pins the tensors
findings.claim: `del model` and torch.cuda.empty_cache() run inside `except RuntimeError as e`. e.__traceback__ keeps the train_model and _train_step frames alive, including model, opt, ema and the current batch, so nothing they occupy is released, and those tensors stay allocated during the time.sleep(300). When the except block ends they return to PyTorch's reserved pool, but no further empty_cache runs before guard.check(need_vram=True). nvidia-smi then counts this process's own cache as used VRAM.
findings.failure_scenario: On the 8188 MiB card, another application holds 6600 MiB and the ladder's pool is 1500 MiB, so an allocation fails. During the 5-minute wait the other application drops to 5500 MiB. With proper cleanup free VRAM would be 2688 MiB and the retry would pass. With the pool retained it reads 1188 MiB, below MIN_FREE_VRAM_MB. Nothing ever releases the pool, so the guard waits 3600 s and raises ResourceAbort, stopping the ladder although the retry would fit.
findings.suggested_fix: Only record the OOM inside the except block. After it, run del model, gc.collect(), torch.cuda.empty_cache() and then sleep. Calling gc and empty_cache again immediately before the guard check is also sufficient.

votes.reasoning:
The defect is real. I could not refute the mechanism, but the failure scenario's numbers are overstated, so the false abort happens in a narrower range than the report describes.

TRACE (paths under C:/Users/user/massive_joint_nlu/.review_snapshot)
1. An OOM in _train_step, predict or model.to propagates out of train_model and is caught at src/experiment.py:139. "CUDA out of memory" passes the filter on line 140, so lines 143-145 run while e is still bound.
2. e.__traceback__ holds the frames of run, train_model, _train_step, _forward_loss and forward. The train_model frame holds the same model object (train.py:144, Module.to returns self), plus opt, sched, ema, counts and b. So `del model` on line 143 only removes run's own name.
3. torch.cuda.empty_cache on line 144 only touches unoccupied memory. The docstring at torch/cuda/memory.py:114 says it "Releases all unoccupied cached memory" so it becomes visible in nvidia-smi. Pinned tensors therefore stay allocated through time.sleep(300), and cached memory counts as used in nvidia-smi until it is released.
4. A stdlib simulation with the same frame and closure shape (Python 3.10.4, gc disabled) showed nothing freed by `del model` and nothing freed during the block. Everything was freed at the end of the block, so refcounting alone does it.
5. I found no cycles that would delay this. models.py has no hooks or closures over self, and the LR scheduler holds the optimizer by weakref (lr_scheduler.py:55-57).
6. After the block the tensors return to the allocator's cache. Grep finds empty_cache only at experiment.py:144 and :191, and gc.collect nowhere.
7. Everything before the guard is CPU only: seed_everything, build_model, init_from. guard.check at train.py:141 runs before model.to at :144, and guard._gpu computes free VRAM as total - memory.used, so the process's own cache counts as used.
8. The guard wait loop only sleeps. After MAX_WAIT_S (3600 s) it raises ResourceAbort, line 140 re-raises it, and run_ladder.py:280 exits with code 3.

WHERE THE REPORT OVERSTATES
Line 144 does release every fully free cached segment. What stays reserved is therefore the set pinned at the exception, not the peak pool. Estimated upper bounds for that set are below (B=64, median batch-max T=17, train max T=35). My parameter formula reproduces the real Stage-1 count of 4,344,472 exactly.
- Stage-1 size: 156-250 MiB
- tfm256x6: 220-362 MiB
- ext46k: 208-303 MiB
- tfm384x6: 419-662 MiB
- tfm384x6 + R-Drop + EMA: 696-1182 MiB

Segment fragmentation can add somewhat to these, and a biaffine head adds roughly 115 MiB per forward pass. So a retained 1500 MiB looks out of reach for these configurations.

At the scenario's 5500 MiB, a Stage-1-size run reads about 8188-5500-250 = 2438 MiB, less CUDA context overhead C, and the guard passes. The quoted 1188 MiB reading and abort do not happen as written for those sizes. The 2688 MiB "clean" figure also ignores C, which no cleanup can free.

The false block is real for other-app usage O in the range (6688-C-P, 6688-C], where P is the retained pool, so the band is P MiB wide. Example with P=250, ignoring C: O=6500 reads 1438 MiB when a clean process would read 1688 MiB. The guard pauses, and if O stays there for 3600 s the ladder stops with ResourceAbort even though the retry would fit.

findings.title: Result files are not written atomically on a machine with unclean reboots
findings.claim: dev_metrics.json is written in place by write_text with no flush, fsync or rename, and train.py:179 overwrites the checkpoint in place. rebuild_leaderboard parses every metrics file with no error handling (experiment.py:28), and the resume check at line 111 tests only that the .pt exists. On restart the first rebuild_leaderboard, reached through best() or the end of run(), raises JSONDecodeError, and the ladder cannot run until a person deletes that file. If only the .pt is truncated while the metrics survive, the run counts as already done and the corruption surfaces only when that checkpoint is reloaded for final evaluation.

findings.claim: NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=1) on (n_tokens, n_gold_slots) returns the same pool utterance for identical queries. The notebook uses the same one-neighbour method with scaled features, so its tie-breaking is not guaranteed to match.

def matched_control(merged):
    """No-Train-OOV control for Slot-Train-OOV: every pool utterance at the same (n_tokens, n_gold_slots)
    counts, weighted so each key carries its Slot-Train-OOV count. A key absent from the pool uses its nearest key(s)."""
    slot = merged[merged["train_oov_group"] == "Slot-Train-OOV"]
    pool = merged[merged["train_oov_group"] == "No-Train-OOV"]
    feats = ["n_tokens", "n_gold_slots"]
    pool_x = pool[feats].to_numpy()
    tp = fp = fn = 0.0
    for key, weight in slot[feats].value_counts().items():
        d = ((pool_x - np.array(key)) ** 2).sum(1)
        near = pool[d == d.min()]
        a, b, c = slot_counts(near["gold_tags"], near["pred_tags"])
        share = weight / len(near)
        tp, fp, fn = tp + a * share, fp + b * share, fn + c * share
    f_m = 100.0 * 2 * tp / (2 * tp + fp + fn)
    f_s = metrics_from_frame(slot)["slot_micro_f1"]
    return {"matched_no_oov_f1": f_m, "slot_oov_f1": f_s, "gap": f_m - f_s,

```python
def matched_control(merged):
    """No-Train-OOV slot F1 reweighted to the Slot-Train-OOV mix of (length, #slots). Each query uses ALL pool
    rows at its minimum standardised distance, each weighted 1/k, so row order cannot change the result."""
    slot = merged[merged["train_oov_group"] == "Slot-Train-OOV"]
    pool = merged[merged["train_oov_group"] == "No-Train-OOV"]
    feats = ["n_tokens", "n_gold_slots"]
    Xs, Xp = slot[feats].to_numpy(float), pool[feats].to_numpy(float)
    sd = np.vstack([Xs, Xp]).std(0)
    sd[sd == 0] = 1.0
    c = np.array([slot_counts([g], [p]) for g, p in zip(pool["gold_tags"], pool["pred_tags"])], float)
    tot = np.zeros(3)
    for q in Xs:
        d = (((Xp - q) / sd) ** 2).sum(1)
        tot += c[d <= d.min() + 1e-9].mean(0)
    tp, fp, fn = tot
    f_m = 100.0 * 2 * tp / max(2 * tp + fp + fn, 1e-9)
    f_s = metrics_from_frame(slot)["slot_micro_f1"]
    return {"matched_no_oov_f1": f_m, "slot_oov_f1": f_s, "gap": f_m - f_s,
            "avg_tokens": float(slot["n_tokens"].mean()), "avg_slots": float(slot["n_gold_slots"].mean())}
```

confirmed.title: OOM retry keeps its own reserved VRAM, so the guard can stall and then stop instead of retrying
confirmed.claim: torch.cuda.empty_cache() runs inside the except block, while e.__traceback__ still pins the train_model frames holding the model, optimiser and batch tensors. `del model` removes only run()'s reference, so nothing is released, including during the 5-minute sleep. Those tensors are freed only when the except block ends, and they go back to PyTorch's cache, which stays reserved. The next attempt calls guard.check(need_vram=True) at src/train.py line 141 before anything else clears the cache. nvidia-smi counts that reserved memory as used (src/guard.py lines 33-34 and 49).
confirmed.failure_scenario: The other GPU job holds most of the VRAM and this process has about 1.7 GB reserved when it hits OOM. On the retry, nvidia-smi reports under 1500 MB free even though this process could reuse its own cache. The guard pauses for up to MAX_WAIT_S, one hour, then raises ResourceAbort and the ladder exits with 'STOPPED SAFELY'. The intended 4-attempt retry never trains again unless the other job frees memory. No results are lost, but the unattended run stops early.
confirmed.suggested_fix: After leaving the except block and before the next attempt, call gc.collect() and then torch.cuda.empty_cache(), or sleep and clear the cache after the block.

votes.reasoning:
Not refuted. The defect is real and "minor" is the right severity, but the harm is narrower than the failure scenario suggests.

**Code trace (snapshot line numbers)**
1. An OOM inside train_model is caught at experiment.py:139. While `e` is bound, e.__traceback__ holds the train_model and _train_step frames. Their locals include model (the same object as run()'s, because .to() returns self at train.py:144), opt, ema, counts, b and loss.
2. Line 143 `del model` drops only run()'s name.
3. Line 144 empty_cache() can only release unoccupied blocks. The installed torch 1.13.1 docstring (cuda/memory.py:114-116) says it "Releases all unoccupied cached memory" so that it becomes "visible in nvidia-smi".
4. Line 145 then sleeps 300 s with all of that memory still allocated.
5. When the except block ends, Python deletes `e`, the frames die and the tensors return to the cache. Reserved memory does not change.
6. The next attempt runs seed_everything (config.py:37-42), build_model (CPU only, models.py:493-499) and, for warm starts, torch.load(map_location="cpu"). It then reaches guard.check(need_vram=True) at train.py:141.
7. The only empty_cache calls in the snapshot are experiment.py:144 and 191, so nothing clears the cache first. need_vram=True also bypasses the throttle (guard.py:58).
8. guard.py:33-34 returns total minus used, and used includes this process's reserved memory. guard.py:49 then adds the "free VRAM" reason.
9. The wait loop at guard.py:66-70 clears nothing and raises ResourceAbort at line 68 after 3600 s. experiment.py:140 re-raises it, and run_ladder.py:280-282 prints STOPPED SAFELY and exits with code 3.

**Check I ran**
I executed the real guard.py source and the real experiment.py lines 127-145 with stubs for nvidia-smi, the clock and the allocator. It was stdlib only and wrote no files. The values were total 8188 MB, other use 6400 MB, and an attempt needing 1900 MB, which hits OOM at 1700 MB reserved.
- **Current code, other job stable:** line 144 leaves reserved at 1700 -> 1700 with 1700 still allocated, and the same holds during the sleep. At the retry, allocated is 0 and reserved is 1700. The guard reports "free VRAM 88 MB" and raises ResourceAbort at t=3930 s.
- **Other job frees 300 MB during the sleep:** the current code sees 388 MB and aborts at t=3930 s. With the fix below it sees 2088 MB and the run completes at t=300 s.
- **Other job frees 1500 MB at t=1000:** the current code resumes and completes at t=1020 s, which matches the report's "unless the other job frees memory".

The allocator and nvidia-smi are modelled from torch's documented behaviour. Nothing ran on the GPU, as the limits require.

**Where the report overstates**
- Let F be the free VRAM with this process's cache empty, and R its reserved memory at OOM. The bug changes the outcome only when F >= 1500 and F - R < 1500.
- With a stable other job, OOM implies R is about F and at least 1500 MB, so only heavy variants can reach this case. The Stage-1-sized model has 4.34M parameters (ladder_A.log), and I estimate it reserves a few hundred MB. That is not measured, and the logs record no VRAM figures.
- If the other job grew instead, F is about R and below 1500 right after the OOM. The guard blocks with or without a fix, and the bug only means the other job must give back R more.
- With a stable other job and the same seed and memory demand, a retry OOMs again. In the stub with the fix, that gave three more OOMs and a plain RuntimeError at t=900 s. run_ladder.py catches only ResourceAbort, so that ends in a traceback rather than STOPPED SAFELY.
- So the real harm is the partial-easing case, where the other job frees a little, not the stable case in the report. No results are lost either way, and finished runs are skipped on restart.

Besides the snapshot, I read those logs (read-only) and the installed torch sources.

In src/experiment.py, add `import gc` and move lines 143-145 out of the except block, so the cleanup runs after `e` and its traceback are gone:

            model, ckpt = train_model(model, ctx.assets, ds["train"], ds["dev"], tcfg, name, meta=meta, verbose=verbose)
            break
        except RuntimeError as e:
            if isinstance(e, guard.ResourceAbort) or "out of memory" not in str(e).lower() or attempt == 3:
                raise
            print(f"[{name}] GPU out of memory, waiting 5 minutes before retry {attempt + 1}", flush=True)

confirmed.title: Guard resume requires 76 C even when heat was not the cause
confirmed.claim: The wait loop always calls _reasons(need_vram, cooling=True), so every pause, including one caused only by RAM or VRAM, can end only at GPU temperature <= RESUME_TEMP_C. That is stricter than the 86 C limit under which training was allowed to run. Idle cooling normally clears this, but another load on the GPU does not.
confirmed.failure_scenario: A second GPU process keeps the card at 80 C. Available RAM dips to 850 MB at an epoch end, causing "pausing (low RAM 850 MB)". RAM recovers to 1.5 GB a minute later, but 80 > 76 keeps the loop waiting. After 3600 s, ResourceAbort reports "still unsafe (GPU 80C)", the ladder exits with code 3, the current run is lost and nothing restarts it. In rung A the restart also triggers the base change. The same happens for a VRAM pause at run start.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Use the cooling limit only if temperature was among the reasons when the pause began. Otherwise keep comparing against MAX_TEMP_C while waiting for RAM or VRAM.

votes.reasoning:
The defect is real, and "minor" is the right severity.

Trace with the reported values (card at 80 C, RAM 850 MB, then 1500 MB):
1. train.py:241 calls guard.check(run_name). need_vram is False. The call is not throttled if 20 s have passed since the last check.
2. guard.py:61 calls _reasons(False, cooling=False). 850 < 900 adds "low RAM 850 MB". The limit is 86 and 80 >= 86 is false, so there is no GPU reason. Line 65 prints "pausing (low RAM 850 MB)".
3. guard.py:70 hard-codes cooling=True. RAM at 1500 MB clears, but the limit is now 76 and 80 > 76, so reasons becomes ["GPU 80C"]. The loop continues at a temperature the entry check had just accepted.
4. guard.py:67-68 raises ResourceAbort on the first poll after 3600 s.
5. The exception passes through the try/finally at train.py:206-243, is re-raised at experiment.py:139-141, and run_ladder.py:280-282 prints STOPPED SAFELY and exits with code 3.
6. On restart, experiment.py:111 needs dev_metrics.json, which is only written at line 185 after training finishes, so the run retrains from epoch 0. The project has no .ps1, .bat, .cmd or .sh wrapper that would restart it.

Simulation: I executed the real guard.py source with fake psutil, subprocess and time on a virtual clock, in memory only, with nothing written to the project.
- This scenario aborted at t=3630 s with "RUN: still unsafe after 3600s (GPU 80C)".
- The VRAM variant (train.py:141, need_vram=True, free VRAM 1000 then 3000 MB, 80 C) aborted the same way.

The "working as designed" defence does not hold. The docstring promises a stop only if "the condition does not clear". Here the condition did clear, and the same 80 C was acceptable while training ran. The smoke test has no guard coverage.

What limits the impact:
- It needs a foreign GPU load holding the card at 77-85 C for the whole hour. Without one the card idles down and the only cost is a longer pause (simulated: 600 s instead of 60 s).
- results/ladder_A.log has no [guard] line so far, so this has not fired.
- The lost run is cheap: stored metrics show about 100-190 s per run. The real cost is a one-hour stall, then a ladder that stays stopped.
- The VRAM variant is narrower: the other process must release VRAM yet keep the card hot.
- The claim's "can end only at <= 76 C" has one exception. _gpu() returns (None, None) on any nvidia-smi failure, so a single failed poll skips the temperature test. This does not refute the claim.

The rung A sub-claim holds on current results. Log line 141 shows base A1_fresh_lr5e-4 at 79.10, and results now contain A2_rare1 at 79.73. A restart's best("A") at run_ladder.py:142 would pick A2_rare1, and screen() would then retrain the other A2_ variants because their configuration no longer matches. This fires on any rung A restart once a finished A2 run beats A1. It is a separate defect in run_ladder.py, and the guard fix does not remove it.

Not verified: real card temperatures under a foreign load. I did not query the hardware, per the task limits; only the presence of nvidia-smi.exe was confirmed. The trigger temperatures are the claim's scenario values.

Latch the cooling state in check(), replacing the wait loop at guard.py:66-70. Nothing else changes.

    cooling = False
    while reasons:
        if time.time() - start > MAX_WAIT_S:
            raise ResourceAbort(f"{tag}: still unsafe after {MAX_WAIT_S}s ({', '.join(reasons)})")
        cooling = cooling or any(r.startswith("GPU") for r in reasons)
        time.sleep(30)

Simulated with a RAM pause at 85 C, 90 C mid-wait, then 80 C with RAM recovered at 180 s, the reviewer's version resumes at 180 s at 80 C. The latched version treats that as a heat pause and keeps waiting for <= 76 C.

- VRAM pause at 80 C: resumes at 60 s.
- Heat pause 88 C, then steady 80 C: still aborts at 3630 s, as designed.

confirmed.title: GPU OOM cleanup runs while the traceback still pins the tensors
confirmed.claim: `del model` and torch.cuda.empty_cache() run inside `except RuntimeError as e`. e.__traceback__ keeps the train_model and _train_step frames alive, including model, opt, ema and the current batch, so nothing they occupy is released, and those tensors stay allocated during the time.sleep(300). When the except block ends they return to PyTorch's reserved pool, but no further empty_cache runs before guard.check(need_vram=True). nvidia-smi then counts this process's own cache as used VRAM.
confirmed.failure_scenario: On the 8188 MiB card, another application holds 6600 MiB and the ladder's pool is 1500 MiB, so an allocation fails. During the 5-minute wait the other application drops to 5500 MiB. With proper cleanup free VRAM would be 2688 MiB and the retry would pass. With the pool retained it reads 1188 MiB, below MIN_FREE_VRAM_MB. Nothing ever releases the pool, so the guard waits 3600 s and raises ResourceAbort, stopping the ladder although the retry would fit.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Only record the OOM inside the except block. After it, run del model, gc.collect(), torch.cuda.empty_cache() and then sleep. Calling gc and empty_cache again immediately before the guard check is also sufficient.

votes.reasoning:
The defect is real. I could not refute the mechanism, but the failure scenario's numbers are overstated, so the false abort happens in a narrower range than the report describes.

TRACE (paths under C:/Users/user/massive_joint_nlu/.review_snapshot)
1. An OOM in _train_step, predict or model.to propagates out of train_model and is caught at src/experiment.py:139. "CUDA out of memory" passes the filter on line 140, so lines 143-145 run while e is still bound.
2. e.__traceback__ holds the frames of run, train_model, _train_step, _forward_loss and forward. The train_model frame holds the same model object (train.py:144, Module.to returns self), plus opt, sched, ema, counts and b. So `del model` on line 143 only removes run's own name.
3. torch.cuda.empty_cache on line 144 only touches unoccupied memory. The docstring at torch/cuda/memory.py:114 says it "Releases all unoccupied cached memory" so it becomes visible in nvidia-smi. Pinned tensors therefore stay allocated through time.sleep(300), and cached memory counts as used in nvidia-smi until it is released.
4. A stdlib simulation with the same frame and closure shape (Python 3.10.4, gc disabled) showed nothing freed by `del model` and nothing freed during the block. Everything was freed at the end of the block, so refcounting alone does it.
5. I found no cycles that would delay this. models.py has no hooks or closures over self, and the LR scheduler holds the optimizer by weakref (lr_scheduler.py:55-57).
6. After the block the tensors return to the allocator's cache. Grep finds empty_cache only at experiment.py:144 and :191, and gc.collect nowhere.
7. Everything before the guard is CPU only: seed_everything, build_model, init_from. guard.check at train.py:141 runs before model.to at :144, and guard._gpu computes free VRAM as total - memory.used, so the process's own cache counts as used.
8. The guard wait loop only sleeps. After MAX_WAIT_S (3600 s) it raises ResourceAbort, line 140 re-raises it, and run_ladder.py:280 exits with code 3.

WHERE THE REPORT OVERSTATES
Line 144 does release every fully free cached segment. What stays reserved is therefore the set pinned at the exception, not the peak pool. Estimated upper bounds for that set are below (B=64, median batch-max T=17, train max T=35). My parameter formula reproduces the real Stage-1 count of 4,344,472 exactly.
- Stage-1 size: 156-250 MiB
- tfm256x6: 220-362 MiB
- ext46k: 208-303 MiB
- tfm384x6: 419-662 MiB
- tfm384x6 + R-Drop + EMA: 696-1182 MiB

Segment fragmentation can add somewhat to these, and a biaffine head adds roughly 115 MiB per forward pass. So a retained 1500 MiB looks out of reach for these configurations.

At the scenario's 5500 MiB, a Stage-1-size run reads about 8188-5500-250 = 2438 MiB, less CUDA context overhead C, and the guard passes. The quoted 1188 MiB reading and abort do not happen as written for those sizes. The 2688 MiB "clean" figure also ignores C, which no cleanup can free.

The false block is real for other-app usage O in the range (6688-C-P, 6688-C], where P is the retained pool, so the band is P MiB wide. Example with P=250, ignoring C: O=6500 reads 1438 MiB when a clean process would read 1688 MiB. The guard pauses, and if O stays there for 3600 s the ladder stops with ResourceAbort even though the retry would fit.

SEVERITY
Minor is fair. The abort needs three things in sequence:
- an OOM after passing the 1500 MiB check (results/ladder_A.log has no OOM or guard lines so far);
- a partial drop into that narrow band;
- about an hour staying there.

The result is a clean exit 3 with finished runs kept, though an unattended ladder then stays stopped until someone restarts it. There is also a second effect the report only implies: during the 300 s sleep the pinned VRAM is withheld from the other process at its tightest moment, which is what guard.py exists to avoid. tools/smoke.py has no coverage of this path (a grep for oom, guard, retry and empty_cache finds nothing).

NOT VERIFIED
Under the hard limits I ran no torch and no nvidia-smi.
- The simulation uses stand-in objects, not real tensors.
- VRAM sizes are computed estimates, not measurements.
- The stub for _OutOfMemoryError shows no base class. Its being a RuntimeError subclass, which line 139 relies on, comes from my knowledge of PyTorch's source, not from anything I could read here. torch 1.13.1 is what `python` on PATH resolves to; I could not confirm the ladder uses that interpreter.

Nothing in the project was changed.
votes.better_fix:
Move the cleanup out of the except block in src/experiment.py and add `import gc` at the top:

        try:
            model, ckpt = train_model(model, ctx.assets, ds["train"], ds["dev"], tcfg, name, meta=meta, verbose=verbose)
            break
        except RuntimeError as e:
            if isinstance(e, guard.ResourceAbort) or "out of memory" not in str(e).lower() or attempt == 3:
                raise
            print(f"[{name}] GPU out of memory, waiting 5 minutes before retry {attempt + 1}", flush=True)
        # Outside the except block: e and its traceback are gone, so train_model's tensors are unreferenced.
        del model
        gc.collect()
        torch.cuda.empty_cache()
        time.sleep(300)

I ran this control flow in a stdlib simulation on four paths: OOM then success, non-OOM error, ResourceAbort after OOM, and four OOMs. It behaved correctly on all of them, and everything was freed before the sleep. It has not been run against real torch objects.

Prefer this to the report's alternative of calling gc and empty_cache just before the guard check. That alternative fixes the guard reading but still holds the pinned VRAM through the 5-minute sleep. gc.collect() was not needed for the objects I traced, since refcounting alone freed them. I would keep it as one cheap defensive line because I could not exercise real torch objects here.

confirmed.title: Result files are not written atomically on a machine with unclean reboots
confirmed.claim: dev_metrics.json is written in place by write_text with no flush, fsync or rename, and train.py:179 overwrites the checkpoint in place. rebuild_leaderboard parses every metrics file with no error handling (experiment.py:28), and the resume check at line 111 tests only that the .pt exists. This falls short of the module docstring's claim that a crash never loses a finished run.
confirmed.failure_scenario: An unclean reboot in the seconds after a run finishes leaves dev_metrics.json empty or NUL-filled. On restart the first rebuild_leaderboard, reached through best() or the end of run(), raises JSONDecodeError, and the ladder cannot run until a person deletes that file. If only the .pt is truncated while the metrics survive, the run counts as already done and the corruption surfaces only when that checkpoint is reloaded for final evaluation.

- If an A1 candidate is unfinished, a restart trains it first and dies at line 186, so it does not reach best(). That run is kept, because line 185 comes first.
